Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women remain a contender in deeper Pac-12 Conference | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
Editor’s note: This is the fifth and final story in a series examining the offseason for the Gonzaga women’s basketball program.

It’s not anywhere close to the original, but for the Gonzaga women’s basketball program the refashioned Pac-12 Conference that it will now call home will present plenty of challenges.

More so than the West Coast Conference – although the Zags’ final season in the WCC was arguably their most entertaining and tightly contested ever.

The WCC has historically been light on competitive depth. Last season was an outlier. Most years two, maybe three teams challenged for league and conference tournament championships.

The respect Gonzaga forged in the WCC will likely follow it into the Pac-12. In way-too-early 2027 NCAA Tournament bracketology, the Zags are picked to earn the automatic bid from the Pac-12.

The Zags are seeded anywhere from No. 7 to No. 10 in early 2027 NCAA Tournament brackets.

Of the nine Pac-12 teams, Gonzaga (24-10), Colorado State (27-8), Oregon State (23-12) and San Diego State (27-6) are expected to jockey for spots in the top four. But Washington State (9-25) and Boise State (25-9) will definitely have a say in how things play out.

San Diego State won the Mountain West regular-season title last year and Colorado State won the conference tournament to earn a bid to the NCAA Tournament.

“The level of play is going to be high and it’s going to be a very competitive conference season,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said.

Fresno State (15-18), Utah State (6-24) and Texas State (11-19) will likely finish in the lower third. Utah State tied for last in the Mountain West last season, and Fresno State and Texas State have new coaches.

“We’re going to get to play each other twice which is not all that common anymore,” Fortier said. “The Power 4 (conferences) don’t do that. And we didn’t do that in the WCC last year. We’ll get a true (regular-season) champion. I’m looking forward to that. We’re going to be pushed every night.”

The conference tournament format will be just like the WCC with the top two seeds receiving double byes to the semifinals and the No. 3 and No. 4 teams getting byes to the quarterfinals.

Of the new teams, Gonzaga is most familiar with Colorado State. The Zags lost in overtime two years ago in Ft. Collins, Colorado, and fell 70-66 at McCarthey Athletic Center last year.

“They’re tough every year,” Fortier said. “They’ve always been a contender to win the Mountain West.”

San Diego State returns four starters and Oregon State returns three from last year and a fourth who started two years ago is back after sitting out following knee surgery.

Washington State returns all of its starters and a sixth who started 20 games.

Based on the final NET rankings from 2025-26, the new fangled Pac-12 will be much stronger than the WCC.

Here were the final NET rankings for the teams that will comprise the Pac-12: Gonzaga (62), SDSU (66), Colorado State (67), OSU (85), Boise State (120), Fresno State (173), WSU (227), Texas State (251).

Here were the final NET rankings for the remaining WCC teams: Santa Clara (80), Loyola Marymount (108), Pepperdine (132), Portland (134), San Francisco (157), Saint Mary’s (183), Pacific (208), San Diego (268) and Seattle U (342). Denver (293) joins the WCC this fall.

Transfer portal, eligibility, recruiting

Gonzaga has had to use the transfer portal to fill roster holes the last two years. But Fortier hopes it will be a supplemental part of recruiting moving forward.

While many programs across the nation are leaning heavily into the transfer portal to sustain or improve, Fortier wants to resist the temptation. Gonzaga has been built on signing high school players and developing them. She doesn’t plan to deter from the formula.

“We’re pretty excited that we can finally do some building,” Fortier said. “It’s really challenging nowadays where you’re just reorganizing and trying to figure out who you have and what they can do with the way the transfer portal has been. It’s been so discombobulated.”

Fortier doesn’t have to harken back too far to recall the most recent team she developed largely through high school signings. The 2023-24 team, which posted the best record in school history (32-4), started five seniors, four in a fifth year who had signed with Gonzaga out of high school. Whether that can happen again remains to be seen.

The recent change in eligibility rules means it could be at least another two years before Gonzaga dips deep into the high school pool.

The new age-based eligibility the NCAA adopted beginning in 2026-27 allows athletes five years of eligibility to be completed within a strict five-year period. Returning players are grandfathered into the new rule and receive an additional year of eligibility unless they’ve already used a redshirt or medical waiver.

Fortier said 11 of 12 players on her roster are eligible for an additional year. The exception is sophomore Lauren Whittaker, who has exhausted a redshirt and medical waiver.

The Zags have four seniors on the 2026-27 roster – Taylor Smith, Zeryhia Aokuso, McKynnlie Dalan and incoming transfer Jocelyn Medina. Fortier said she will determine which players want to return for another season at a later date.

Gonzaga has an oral commitment from Gonzaga Prep point guard Alyah Cornwall for the 2027 recruiting class. At this point Cornwall is the lone commitment for the early signing period in November.

The 5-foot-8 Cornwall is a true point guard – pass first, score second. It’s been a few years since the Zags had a point guard with a quarterback mindset.

Still, Cornwall can score. In 28 games last year at G-Prep, she averaged 17.9 points, 9.9 rebounds, 5.3 assists and 3.3 steals. She was the Greater Spokane League most valuable player and defensive player of the year.

“She loves getting other people involved,” Bullpups coach Geoff Arte said. “But she can really score it too and finishes around the rim. She loves to push the basketball and get it up ahead.”

Fortier said she’s not certain if she’ll sign others. NCAA rules allow schools to have 15 athletes on scholarship. With 12 players Fortier has some options.

Nonconference

Gonzaga will have fewer conference games than it has had in the WCC with just nine teams in the Pac-12.

Additionally, the NCAA expanded the number of games schools can play from 31 to 32. With 16 conference games that means Gonzaga has scheduled 16 nonconference contests.

Gonzaga is finalizing many of its nonconference games including a tournament in Hawaii where the Zags will take on Cal on Nov. 23.

What is known is Gonzaga opens the season at home Nov. 2 against North Dakota State, a return game from a year ago when the Zags opened at NDSU. Nov. 2 is the earliest date any colleges can play this season.

Another announced opponent is Michigan State in a neutral court matchup with the Gonzaga and Michigan State men Dec. 19 in Palm Springs, California.

The Zags will complete a two-year agreement with Arizona State, traveling to Tempe, Arizona, on Dec. 6.

A familiar nonconference opponent returns to the schedule with Montana, which visits Gonzaga Nov. 18. It’ll be an interesting matchup considering the Grizzlies picked up former Gonzaga guard Paige Lofing in the transfer portal this spring.

Those are the known dates at this time. Gonzaga will travel to Stanford and also will play Eastern Washington.

Gonzaga will also have return games at home against UC Riverside and at Grand Canyon.

“I think it’s really going to be a tough (nonconference) schedule,” Fortier said. “We have a couple of really hard games. But I think this team is up for it.”

Another Fortier milestone

Fortier tied LSU coach Kim Mulkey as the fastest coach to reach 300 career victories last season.

Looking back, Fortier said reaching 300 wins didn’t mean much to her.

“I’m just happy for the players and for the (assistant) coaches,” Fortier said. “We care more about how many weddings we get to go to and which babies we get to hold and which players come back. We like to watch them be successful in their life (after basketball).”

Whether she likes it or not, Fortier is closing on another milestone and it’ll happen quickly in the 2026-27 season. Going into her 13th season with her faithful assistants who include her husband Craig, Stacy Clinesmith and Jordan Green – each of whom have been around as long as she has – Lisa Fortier will become Gonzaga’s all-time winningest coach.

She has a 313-84 record (.788 winning percentage). She’s four wins from passing Kelly Graves, who she succeeded. Graves was 316-186 (.699) in 14 seasons.

“I would just say that I’m just grateful to have been part of the building of the program and get us to that place where we were able to just continue and take it to the next level,” Fortier said. “And now I’m ready for us to hopefully take what we’ve done to the next level as well.”

Gonzaga.title: 'Man, it's going to pass.' New Gonzaga wing Chauncey Wiggins navigated summer of uncertainty before earning fifth year
Gonzaga.summary:
Chauncey Wiggins gave Florida State’s upset bid a jolt of life with 37 seconds left during an ACC Tournament quarterfinal game against top-ranked Duke last March.

With the Seminoles trailing 80-77, Wiggins received the ball on the right corner and went to work on Duke’s Cameron Boozer, backing the Naismith Award winner down until he got to his spot outside of the paint. That’s when Wiggins used his long frame to pull up over the sturdy, 6-foot-10 center, and sink a 13-foot step back shot that trimmed the Blue Devils’ lead to one.

The clutch jumper represented the 967th and 968th points of Wiggins’ career – the last ones he’d score as a college basketball player. Or so he thought.

Florida State came out on the wrong end against Duke, losing 80-79, and subsequently turned down an invitation to play in the NIT, signaling the end of Wiggins’ college journey.

The wing was prepared to turn the page, fulfilled with how his four college seasons played out. He made consecutive NCAA Tournament appearances at Clemson, playing key bench minutes for the 2023-24 team that advanced to the Elite Eight. Under first-year Florida State coach Luke Loucks, he averaged double figures for a group that claimed the Seminoles’ first winning ACC record since 2020-21. He nearly eclipsed the 1,000-point milestone, posted a career win-loss record of 92-45 and earned academic honors at Clemson in 2024.

An All-ACC selection would’ve been a nice bonus, but outside of that Wiggins didn’t have too many complaints with his college resume.

“I thought college was over,” Wiggins said. “I thought it was a good four years. Making it to March Madness, that was my dream. I wish I’d gotten on the All-ACC team but I didn’t. I thought my college career was done.”

As Wiggins went through the pre-NBA draft process, there were murmurs that he and other class of 2022 high school graduates might have another shot to play college ball through the NCAA’s new age-based eligibility rules, permitting student-athletes to play five seasons over five years.

Wiggins didn’t think much of it as he traveled for NBA workouts with the Miami Heat, Los Angeles Lakers, Phoenix Suns, Sacramento Kings and Dallas Mavericks, eventually latching on with the Boston Celtics for NBA Summer League in Las Vegas.

“I literally kept telling one of my friends, ‘This thing ain’t going to happen at all, we’re not getting another year,’” Wiggins said. “Then a few weeks after that, our class didn’t get grandfathered in. So we were like, yeah it’s done.”

One friend, former Utah State guard MJ Collins Jr., was insistent, telling Wiggins, “Man, it’s going to pass.”

Not long after he completed his Summer League assignment with the Celtics, Wiggins returned home to Atlanta and began to monitor the college basketball news cycle, eventually learning Collins Jr., new Gonzaga point guard Javon Bennett – a transfer from Dayton – and other players in Ohio had challenged the NCAA in court to secure another year of eligibility.

Wiggins got together with family members, his agent and a lawyer to explore the possibilities, eventually joining a separate group of fifth-year hopefuls seeking a similar injunction in his home state of Georgia.

After finishing a workout on July 31, Wiggins opened up social media and learned about the class-wide injunction in Colorado that granted fifth-year seniors in all sports an extra year of eligibility. Less than a week later, a state judge ruled in favor of Wiggins and other players who filed in Georgia, giving the transfer wing another layer of security.

“So I’m kind of double-protected, if that makes sense,” Wiggins said.

Before either ruling, Wiggins was already hearing from high-major college programs around the country, including Gonzaga, Georgia, SMU, Washington and the Florida State program he recently played for. Wiggins also had pro options on the table, including a G League offer from the Kings and an opportunity with a club team in Japan’s top league.

At Gonzaga, his point of contact was assistant coach RJay Barsh, who worked on Leonard Hamilton’s staff at Florida State in 2022-23. Wiggins and Barsh didn’t overlap in Tallahassee, but the Gonzaga assistant was familiar with the wing’s game from Florida State’s encounters with Clemson in the ACC. It also helped they had a mutual friend in FSU assistant Director of basketball operations Ryan Shnider, a former graduate assistant under Hamilton who stayed on staff when the Seminoles hired Loucks.

“From a basketball standpoint, (Barsh) was recruiting me just saying you’re going to play 2, 3, 4 here,” said Wiggins, who primarily played the 4 and occasionally as small-ball 5 at his last two schools. “Even when he said the 2, I was kind of surprised. … He was like, we’ve got some good length and good guys here. He said we have positions but just say if you get the rebound, you’re going to push the ball and now you have to know what to call. Then obviously coaches can say that and not mean it. Obviously I’m an older guy so I know what I want. Also I had to ask him, can I see some clips of this?”

Shnider also had a relationship with Jalen Warley, who successfully made a similar transition from Florida State to Gonzaga, where he was one of Mark Few’s most valuable two-way players during last year’s 31-win campaign. Wiggins reached out to Warley to get an honest and transparent evaluation of Gonzaga’s program, coaching staff and culture.

“He really loved it there,” Wiggins said. “He really loved it, had a lot to say about the coaches in a positive way. I was like, hey just be realistic. He was like the coaches, what they say is true basically.”

An Atlanta native who’s only resided in Georgia, South Carolina and Florida, Wiggins was familiar with Gonzaga but couldn’t have identified Spokane on a map of Washington. (He admits he originally thought it was a suburb of Seattle). By the time he was born in 2004, the Zags had already planted their flag on the national stage, and Wiggins became accustomed to hearing the school’s name every year, usually whenever March rolled around.

“I watched Gonzaga when I got into college and when I was in high school, but even when I was a kid I always heard of some school called Gonzaga,” Wiggins said. “They always make it to March Madness, they always win, they’re always putting people in the pros, they have a good coach.”

A 13.3 point-per-game scorer last season at Florida State who made 38.7% of his 3-pointers, Wiggins is encouraged by all the possibilities at Gonzaga. The 6-10 wing has seen and enjoyed the online discourse about potential lineups featuring him next to 6-7 Davis Fogle, 6-11 Braden Huff and 7-1 Massamba Diop.

“That was really (Barsh’s) pitch and saying, with your shooting ability, we’re adding your shooting ability so that’s really going to open up things for everybody on the floor, whether that’s your shooting or B-Huff’s hook shot or Diop, with them doubling the center,” Wiggins said. “It’s just going to open up a lot. Coach Few’s system, a lot of movement, not really standing in the corner. It was a really good pitch and obviously it got me here.”

Wiggins plans to spend the next few weeks working out back home in Atlanta with a longtime personal trainer, “Coach BB” of SmallBall Training, and shooting coach Bobby Perez before moving to Spokane ahead of fall practices.

On the surface, outside shooting projects to be the most valuable asset Wiggins will bring to a Gonzaga program that posted the lowest 3-point percentage of Few’s 27-year tenure last season (34.0%). Wiggins wants to keep that aspect of his offensive game sharp, but the veteran wing is also looking to improve his ball-handling and defense.

“I’m really showing people I can be even more versatile, really just working on putting the ball on the floor more,” Wiggins said. “Rebounding more, crashing offense, defense. I’m always still working on my defense. Offense, just putting the ball on the floor, making sure the shooting is staying sharp, post game if I ever need to and touch around the basket.”

Washington State.title: After blowout win over Duquesne, what’s the status of WSU’s special teams unit?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Early in the week, when Washington State coach Kirby Moore was discussing a recent loss and looking ahead to his team’s next game, he considered how his guys could absorb the loss of receiver Tony Freeman.

Freeman is set to miss the rest of the season with an injury, so others would have to step up. What about speedy wideout Tank Hawkins? Could the Cougars find a spot for him?

“We have to,” Moore said.

What Moore probably couldn’t have predicted was the way Hawkins got involved. In the fourth quarter of WSU’s 48-7 win over Duquesne on Saturday afternoon, he took a punt back 65 yards for a touchdown, jetting around defenders on his way to the end zone. It amounted to a perfect use of Hawkins’ skillset.

Except that wasn’t the only damage the Cougars did on special teams in Saturday’s game. One punt return prior, safety Jaylen Thomas returned a punt 47 yards to the house. With back-to-back punt returns for touchdowns, WSU didn’t just register its first of those in a decade. The Cougars also turned in two punt return touchdowns for the first time since 1973.

“Jaylen Thomas, who’s done it on defense, doing it now on special teams. That guy’s special,” Moore said of Thomas, who also picked off two passes against Kansas State last weekend. “Tank Hawkins, really good to see him out in space.”

For WSU, the meaning here goes deeper than just two eye-popping punt returns. The Cougars needed those to resuscitate their special teams unit, which had turned in two forgettable showings to kick off the season, including in losses to Washington and Kansas State. Against UW, the Cougars botched two kick returns. Against K-State, the Cougars allowed a punt return of some 60 yards, which the Wildcats used to set up a short touchdown moments later.

So in that way, Thomas’ and Hawkins’ plays weren’t just fun sequences against an overmatched FCS club like Duquesne. They were also confidence-builders for coach Derek Sage, who mans the team’s special teams unit and wide receivers. No USA Network cameras panned to him in Saturday’s game, but it’s probably fair to say he wore a wide smile after those two returns.

Then there’s the matter of WSU’s placekicking. On Saturday, kicker Jack Stevens misfired on his only field goal attempt of the game, a 30-yard try from the left hash. That makes him 1-for-5 to open the season. He also missed an extra point, the first time he’s done so in his career. His only made field goal has come on a 42-yard connection against UW. Since then, he’s missed three straight field goals.

Earlier in the season, this pattern felt more uncharacteristic than anything. Stevens missed only three field goals last season, going 16-for-19 on the year, and in fall camp this year, he was consistently accurate. But now it’s turned into a significant problem for WSU, which might have to make a change at that position.

“I got a ton of confidence in Jack,” Moore said. “He’s done it throughout the offseason. We gotta look at the whole operation. There’s snap, there’s hold, there’s protection, there’s a lot of pieces to that. Obviously, we gotta improve, and we’re gonna do that.”

Where could the Cougars look? Their other kicker is North Texas transfer Miguel Arenas, who mans the team’s kickoff duties, likely because he has a bigger leg – just not the more accurate one. But now, as Stevens continues to miss the kinds of field goals that looked like chip shots for him last fall, Arenas could be in line for a bigger role.

It’s worth keeping in mind that even after Stevens missed his field goal, coaches kept him in for extra points. And even after he missed one of those, coaches stuck with him. That probably boosted his confidence.

But as WSU prepares for a home showdown with Arizona next week, a primetime tilt on CBS, the Cougars need their best pieces in place. On Saturday, they showed a willingness to make changes by benching left guard Kyle Martin. It’ll be interesting to see if Cougar coaches show the same kind of readiness to do to the same in their placekicking department.

Washington State.title: In WSU’s lopsided win over FCS Duquesne, the Cougars’ halftime adjustments shone brightest | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – If you listened closely during Washington State players’ jog to the locker room, when they were up just one score on winless FCS squad Duquesne here on Saturday afternoon, you would have noticed them.

Boos.

After a hapless two offensive showings to open the season, losing two straight games to open the year for the first time in a decade, WSU needed a sharp offensive showing in Saturday’s game. In the first two quarters, the Cougars failed to deliver. They lost a turnover, missed a field goal and got two touchdowns called back on penalties, heading into halftime facing all the same problems they did in their first two games.

But in the second half, the Cougs kicked their offense into gear and turned a close game into a blowout one week before a home tilt against Arizona.

If there’s anything to take away from Washington State’s 48-7 win over Duquesne, it’s this: The Cougs made adjustments, which was a key reason behind many of their biggest problems on offense in their first two games. They played with tempo, activated their rushing game and bought time for quarterback Caden Pinnick, who supplied the first passing touchdown of his WSU career.

So if you’re looking for an answer to the question that will hover over this game – were the Cougars actually better on offense in this one, or was Duquesne just a bad FCS team? – that’s a good place to start. The Cougs used adjustments to win this game, which is the kind of trend that can travel across the rest of their season. They deserve credit for that, regardless of the opponent.

In particular, offensive coordinator Matt Miller deserves his due. After WSU’s losses to Washington and Kansas State to open this season, he was pilloried. Plenty of that he deserved. Some he didn’t. The most salient criticism he received, though, was his inability to make adjustments in time. His offense looked slow and unimaginative, but the Cougs spent plenty of those two games in theoretical striking distance, which is why it was fair to critique the speed with which he changed things up.

Duquesne had no business sticking around for two quarters, but look at the totality of what WSU accomplished on offense: 316 rushing yards, including 116 from running back Maxwell Woods and another 109 from fellow tailback Kirby Vorhees. The Cougars scored touchdowns on three straight series to open the second half, and they converted 6 of 9 third-down chances, turning around what had been a serious problem. And Pinnick looked far more comfortable in the pocket, thanks in large part to a far better blocking performance from WSU’s offensive line.

The Cougars had two 100-yard rushers for the first time since 2005, and their 316 rushing yards are the program’s most in a single game since the same season.

At the beginning of the game, Moore was seen carrying what looked like a playsheet, which he didn’t do either of the first two games of the season. At the beginning of the week, he said he wanted to help in WSU’s playcalling duties. So what kind of role did he play in the playcalling department on Saturday?

Pinnick said the job still belonged to Miller, while Moore “definitely had some input in it.” For his part, Moore said this: “It was a collaborative effort. Thought everyone did a really good job. Thought Matt called a good game, and we had a lot of good dialogue on the headset. Obviously, the second half having a plan, and then the players did a really good job executing there.”

Whoever was calling plays, some of the best adjustments the Cougars made in this one centered around their ability to simplify things. Pinnick completed 17 of 22 passes and got himself in a rhythm by hitting several quick stick routes and out routes, taking advantage of the cushion the Dukes were giving Cougar receivers. That’s almost certainly something WSU coaches identified on film, and they deserve credit for cashing in when the game arrived.

In Saturday’s second half, the Cougs were also a lot better on first and second down – something they struggled with in their first two games. Here’s a sampling of some first-down plays: Pinnick 12-yard completion to Darrius Clemons. Leo Pulalasi six-yard rush. Pinnick 26-yard rush. Woods 20-yard rush.

As a result, the Cougars faced only two third downs of nine-plus yards. Against K-State, that number was four. Against Washington, that number was two. Throughout the week, Moore sounded a bit like a broken record, indicating his team’s third-down struggles had more to do with low-efficiency plays on first and second down. At least for one week, the Cougs turned that problem around.

In these kinds of situations, it’s easy to chalk things up to a rousing halftime speech. That’s not always the case. On Saturday, it might have been. According to defensive end Matyus McLain, defensive tackle Kaden Beatty provided some insight, remembering his 2024 season at Kent State, when FCS St. Francis beat the Golden Flashes.

“Like I told the guys in the edge room,” said McLain, a transfer from FCS Idaho, “I’m like, ‘Last year when I was playing the FBS teams, I was the most excited I’ve ever been in my life. I wanted to prove that I belonged, and those guys have that mindset coming into this game every single time. They want to embarrass you.’ ”

Especially without star receiver and kick returner Tony Freeman, who is set to miss the rest of the season with a torn ACL, the Cougars deserve credit for kicking things into gear on offense in the second half. Their offensive line played a key role, and even on that front, coaches made adjustments. They benched left guard Kyle Martin, who had collected an unsightly overall Pro Football Focus offensive grade of 27.7 through two games, including an 8.7 pass-blocking grade against UW and a 0.0 grade against K-State.

With Martin on the bench, WSU’s offensive line featured left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell. Lester had spent most of his career as a left guard, where he played his best games, and he looked better on the inside. Caldwell, a more natural tackle, came off the bench to play right tackle.

After the game, Moore wouldn’t cop to making that arrangement permanent – “we’re gonna need all six of those guys,” he said – but headed into a home showdown against Arizona next weekend, that idea could have some real legs behind it, especially considering the way those five guys played in WSU’s sterling rushing attack.

“In essence, yes, it was a little bit of a mismatch,” Vorhees said, “but when the O-line is working and the O-line is all stepping to the right direction and all got their hands inside, running their feet, it’s gonna bounce. It’s gonna pop. It’s just the nature of outside zone, but it’s a big testament to these guys because it takes one play, two play, three play, pop – you know? So it’s really the guys getting comfortable with how they’re blocking versus how the defense is moving.”

Next weekend against Arizona, which is expected to be 2-1 by the end of the night, WSU cannot afford to start so slowly. The Cougars won’t be favored, and to pull that upset, they’ll need to be far sharper on offense.

Practically speaking, that means cutting out the penalties – they were dinged for four holding calls, three on tight end Jack Pedersen – and showing more aggressiveness in two-minute situations. When the Cougars got the ball back with about 90 seconds to play on Saturday, they looked content to run out the clock, perhaps costing themselves a chance at scoring right before halftime.

“I need to look at that one more (time),” Moore said. “I do think there was a slippery, slow, fine line with that. We got the ball first to start the second half. I can’t remember the yardage on the first play, but I don’t think it was a second-and-two, and so if you go three-and-out quick there, you might give the ball back to them a little bit quicker than you want to. We have to look at that. I think we could have had a better plan just altogether in that situation.”

But broadly speaking, WSU looked far sharper on offense in this game, which is what the team needed after a lethargic two losses to start the season. To avoid a third next weekend, the Cougars will have to show the same willingness to make adjustments they put on display against Duquesne.

Washington State.title: Washington State's offense finally finds rhythm against overmatched FCS visitor | Instant reactions
Washington State.summary:
The first half was troubling – Washington State couldn’t pull away from a winless FCS team. But the Cougars came out of the locker room with a reinvigorated offense and scored touchdowns on their first three possessions of the second half, and their defense blanked visiting Duquesne from there.

It wasn’t as clean – complete control from start to finish – as the Cougars fanbase would have liked, but WSU eventually overpowered the Dukes and picked up its first victory under coach Kirby Moore, winning its home opener 48-7 on Saturday afternoon at Gesa Field.

Skill players find rhythm

WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick settled in after a nightmarish first two plays – a botched snap resulting in an 11-yard loss and an errant pass that was intercepted.

But the sophomore showed progress later in the first half. An up-tempo passing attack led to Pinnick’s 19-yard scoring run late in the second quarter. Pinnick then led WSU’s best drive of the year to open the second half, firing accurate passes toward the sidelines before tossing his first TD pass in a Cougar uniform.

On WSU’s second series of the third quarter, Pinnick completed passes of 19 and 23 yards before a nice throw to the back of the end zone to Branden Ganashamoorthy, who made a leaping grab for a 10-yard TD. Pinnick wound up completing 17 of 22 passes for 196 yards. He distributed passes to seven different receivers. Ganashamoorthy showed big-play potential. Newcomers Darrius Clemons and Daniel Blood weren’t incredibly productive, but both made some good snags on out routes.

A dominant rushing game helped open things up in the passing game. Maxwell Woods and Kirby Vorhees were excellent, albeit against an overmatched Dukes defense. They combined for 225 yards on 20 carries, ripping off a handful of chunk gains as WSU’s maligned offensive line outmuscled a Duquesne defense that entered the game ranked in the bottom 10 of the FCS in total defense.

The Cougars piled up 316 rushing yards on 40 carries, averaging 7.9 yards per attempt during their most productive game on the ground in 20 years.

Finally, big plays

The Cougs entered the game ranked last in the FBS in total offense and scoring offense. Yes, Duquesne’s is the worst defense WSU will play and it’s tough to gain much intel from a game like this, but it should provide some confidence and function as a learning experience for the Cougars’ new staff. Perhaps they’ll lean more on the ground game and mix up plays with an up-tempo attack.

WSU’s offense was stagnant in its first two games, and for much of the first half in this one. The offense was tagged with back-to-back penalties in the red zone during its third drive, resulting in a missed field goal, and couldn’t string anything together on its next possession, then went conservative on its final first-half series and settled for a 14-7 halftime lead.

But the Cougars came out of the break rejuvenated with a quick pace in their offense. The running game took over. Pinnick had more time. Receivers got more separation, and for the first time this season, the Cougars showed positive flashes offensively, finally giving their fans a number of highlight-reel plays.

WSU finished with five passing plays that gained 15 or more yards, and 12 rushes that gained more than 10 yards, including carries of 58, 45 and 26 yards.

The second-half performance should boost the Cougs’ offensive spirits, but they have to prove they can sustain it against a competitive opponent. They’ll have a chance next weekend when former Pac-12 foe Arizona comes to town.

Defense, returners add highlight plays

After a miserable first two weeks of the season, WSU fans were treated with a fun finish, a rare occurrence in football – back-to-back punts returned for touchdowns.

Reigning Pac-12 Defensive Player of the Week Jaylen Thomas, a Cougar safety, weaved through traffic for a 47-yard punt return touchdown with 5:32 left to play.

About two minutes later, WSU receiver Tank Hawkins found a wide lane and raced past everyone for another punt return TD, this one a 65-yarder. WSU hadn’t returned two punts for TDs in a game since 1973.

WSU got those chances because its defense didn’t allow much of anything to the Dukes in the second half. Duquesne went three-and-out on four of its six second-half possessions, managing just 40 yards on 23 plays.

The Cougs’ defense only really had one major lapse, giving up a 54-yard run that set up a Dukes touchdown in the first quarter. After that, Duquesne’s best drive gained 29 yards, and the visitors finished with 180 total yards.

WSU tallied seven tackles for loss and its first two sacks of the year.

Washington State.title: Washington State running backs provide productive 1-2 punch | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
WSU RB Maxwell Woods

The redshirt sophomore showed elusiveness, vision and big-play ability, breaking off five runs of more than 10 yards – including a 45-yard scamper out of the wildcat formation in the first quarter that set up a touchdown. Woods finished with 116 yards on 11 carries, averaging 10.5 yards per attempt. He also provided a few nice plays on check-down passes, picking up 20 yards on three receptions. It was Woods’ second-highest yardage output of his WSU career, trailing only his 152 yards from scrimmage last year in his breakout performance against Utah State in the Cougars’ Famous Idaho Potato Bowl win.

WSU RB Kirby Vorhees

The Cougs had two 100-yard rushers in the same game for the first time in 21 years. Not to be outdone by his backfield teammate, Vorhees had his most productive performance in a WSU uniform, gaining 109 yards on nine carries with his first two touchdowns of the year. The redshirt junior punched in an 8-yard TD run early in the game after Woods’ explosive carry. Late in the third quarter, Vorhees raced through an outside gap and went untouched for a 58-yard TD, putting WSU up 35-7. It was Vorhees’ first 100-yard rushing game since 2024, when he played for South Dakota State, and the second of his career.

Washington State.title: Second-half takeover showed Washington State's potential as conference play nears | Jacob Thorpe
Washington State.summary:
I really hate to do this.

Most years, I would rather tell my editors to run a blank page in the newspaper than write a column analyzing a 41-point win over an FCS team. Usually I try to provide the reader with something else that is useful in these situations, like a betting column. I actually began today planning to write about the radio broadcast led by Chris King, who is relatively new to the position but is capably upholding the high standard for Washington State University play-by-play professionals.

Because, well, Duquesne is a vastly under-resourced opponent who lost its first two games by a combined score of 104-13. What could be learned from a 48-7 win over such an opponent?

Well, it turns out quite a bit. Because until the second half began, the evidence suggested the Cougars and Dukes were peers. WSU’s offense was just as anemic as it had been in the Apple Cup and at Kansas State, beginning the game with an interception and leading hapless Duquesne just 14-7 at the half.

Surely some WSU fans spent halftime nervously checking the team’s schedule on their phones, calculating the likelihood of an 0-12 season if the team lost to its meagerest opponent.

Caden Pinnick showed some growth off the field this week when he took ownership for a moody, terse news conference following last week’s loss. In the second half he showed some growth on the field.

The offense took off after halftime, scoring touchdowns on the first three drives of the second half. The final WSU score was bolstered by consecutive punt return touchdowns by two different players which is something that you, me, and every person who has ever lived have never seen the Cougars do before.

But the point is, WSU showed over the course of the third quarter that it does indeed have the potential to operate at a higher level than it had been. Yes, the opponent was bad. The opponent was bad in the first half, too. The first half showed that scoring against a bad opponent was perhaps something the offense wasn’t ready to do when it was failing to score against better ones the last two weeks.

Pinnick entered the second half having yet to throw a touchdown but had been intercepted three times. Since, he’s tossed a pair of TDs with no picks. Sure it’s a small sample size, but people who say confidence is a key factor in football success got some evidence.

Back to potential. This is a new offense. New quarterback, new offensive coordinator, new offensive-minded head coach. It was always going to be a process. But what we saw on Saturday is that there is somewhere to go. The training wheels are still on and I’m not sure they would score any more points if they had a rematch against Kansas State tomorrow.

But the Cougars don’t have to play Kansas State again tomorrow, or any other day. They have one more power conference opponent in Arizona next weekend, and then it’s peer schools for the rest of the regular season.

Whether their potential is realized remains to be seen. But on Saturday at least, we got to see what the Cougars offense could become.

Washington State.title: Washington State dominates all phases on way to win against Duquesne | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN — The afternoon sun sparkled on Caden Pinnick, the Washington State quarterback who had endured quite the two weeks to open the season. Dressed in a crimson uniform and a white helmet, Pinnick looked loose as he warmed up here at Gesa Field, the site of his team’s game against Duquesne on Saturday afternoon.

Pinnick and the Cougars’ offense might have been matched up against a winless FCS squad, but because of how much that unit floundered in two losses in coach Kirby Moore’s debut season, they had lots of questions to answer. Could WSU kick its offense into gear and turn in a convincing win over the worst team on their schedule?

The Cougars slogged through a listless first half and took its time answering that question, but thanks to a brilliant second stanza, they answered with an emphatic yes in a 48-7 win over Duquesne, earning Moore his first win at the helm of the program.

WSU used a 34-0 second half to pull away, getting a long touchdown rush from running back Kirby Vorhees and two touchdowns passes from Pinnick, who completed 17 of 22 passes for 196 yards, two scores and one interception, which came on his team’s second play from scrimmage. The hosts also totaled 316 yards on the ground, getting two 100-yard rushers: Maxwell Woods piled up 116 yards and Vorhees added 109, plus Pinnick with 76 yards on 12 carries.

The Cougars piled on in the fourth quarter, getting back-to-back punt returns for touchdowns, the first from safety Jaylen Thomas and the second from receiver Tank Hawkins. Thomas returned his 47 yards and Hawkins returned his 65 yards, giving the Cougs their first punt return touchdown since 2016. It’s also the program’s first time with two in one game since 1973.

Thanks to the Cougars’ defense, which held the winless Dukes scoreless over the final three quarters, WSU had few issues pulling away in the second half. On one sequence, Pinnick found a wide-open tight end Jack Pedersen for a touchdown, and on another, he lasered one to the back of the end zone to fourth-year junior Branden Ganashamoorthy. That was Ganashamoorthy’s first regular-season touchdown at WSU.

Considering the two losses they took to open the season, this victory was just about what the Cougs needed: A sharp offensive outing and a blowout win over a hapless FCS team. WSU (1-2) now heads into next weekend’s home showdown with Arizona riding a healthy dose of momentum.

Still, it wasn’t all roses for the Cougars. On their first offensive play, Pinnick couldn’t handle a high snap, resulting in a big loss. On their second, he threw deep into double coverage, resulting in an interception — his third in as many games. The hosts’ offense looked as hapless as it did in their first two games of the season, road losses to Power 4 foes Washington and Kansas State.

Pinnick’s interception was also WSU’s fifth turnover of the season, joining two fumbles from Vorhees and two other picks from Pinnick.

But this was perhaps an even more poignant sequence: With about 90 seconds until halftime, WSU got the ball back, starting its drive at its own 19. It was a classic two-minute drill situation, and because the Cougars were slated to get the ball to open the second half, they had a chance to double-dip, to begin to pull away before the first half even ended. It felt like a chance for the Cougs to seize control of the game.

Instead, WSU opened with a false start before turning to several inside runs, apparently content to run out the clock before halftime. The Cougs ran Vorhees up the middle on three straight plays. They showed a bit more urgency when the clock ticked under 20 seconds, but all told, it seemed like a signal from WSU coaches about the way they viewed their offense.

It was also another forgettable outing for WSU kicker Jack Stevens. In the second quarter, he missed a 30-yard field goal from the left hash, making him 1-for-5 to start the season. In the fourth frame, he misfired on an extra point, the first one he’s missed in his career. Earlier in the season, it felt uncharacteristic — Stevens missed only three field goals last season, and in fall camp this year, he was consistently accurate — but now it’s turned into a significant problem for WSU.

The Cougars’ other kicker is transfer Miguel Arenas, who normally handles kickoffs. WSU stuck with Stevens for extra points after he missed his earlier field goal, but moving forward, it’ll be interesting to see how coaches manage field goal situations.

Washington State.title: Why Washington State will beat Duquesne | The pick
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Realistically speaking, Washington State won’t be too worried about winning its home opener against FCS Duquesne on Saturday afternoon.

Even sporting an offense that ranks last nationally in total offense and scoring, the Cougars are about 371/2-point favorites, which signals how much the Dukes have struggled so far this fall. They rank just about last in the FCS in several key departments, including scoring offense and scoring defense, permitting an average of 527 yards per game against FBS Air Force and FCS power Youngstown State.

Instead, WSU can begin to win some people back by putting Duquesne away early and cruising to an easy win. There might not be a point margin that could restore fans’ faith in offensive coordinator Matt Miller or the Cougars’ offensive line, the latter of which ranks last in the country in Pro Football Focus’ pass-blocking grades, another indication of how lowly a team Duquesne is. But the Cougs would do well to come as close to doing so as they can.

Look for QB Caden Pinnick and the Cougars to check off a few boxes: improve their third-down efficiency, which ranks among the worst in the country ; keep Pinnick clean and give him time in the pocket ; activate their running game, and get receivers like Daniel Blood and Tank Hawkins going, the latter of whom could play a bigger role in the absence of injured wideout Tony Freeman.

If Washington State can do all that and hold Duquesne to one or two scores on defense, the Cougars can re-establish some momentum around their program. That will be critical going into next weekend, when former Pac-12 foe Arizona returns to Pullman for a primetime tilt on CBS. Until then, the Cougs will have to dismantle a winless Dukes team.

Final score: WSU 41, Duquesne 6

Washington State.title: Washington State's keys to victory against Duquesne | 2-minute drill
Washington State.summary:
Washington State vs. Duquesne

Saturday, 12:30 p.m.

Line: WSU favored by 37½.

TV: USA Network Radio: 920-AM

Key matchup

WSU OL vs. Duquesne defensive front: Above all, in Saturday’s game, the Cougars need a convincing showing on offense. A key reason why they have yet to record one of those this season is because of their offensive line, which currently ranks last nationally in Pro Football Focus’ pass-blocking grades with a figure of 17.3. Whatever that group looks like on Saturday, it needs to give Pinnick time to showcase his talent.

WSU’s coaches made slight adjustments in the second of last week’s loss to Kansas State. They benched starting left guard Kyle Martin (0.0 pass-blocking grade) and cleared the way for right tackle Jonny Lester to move back inside and for right tackle Jaylin Caldwell to come off the bench. Could coaches stick with that lineup, or will they put Lester back at right tackle? In his first year-plus starting, he has logged his best games at left guard, but coaches have liked him better at right tackle this fall.

If the Cougars’ front five can give Pinnick time, the third-year sophomore could open things up for receivers Darrius Clemons, Daniel Blood and Tank Hawkins, the last of whom started last week but played only one snap. With senior wideout Tony Freeman out for the rest of the season due to a torn ACL, the Cougs need a bit more from that trio.

How the Cougs win…

WSU can win this game all kinds of ways, but perhaps the most important could come on offense. The Cougars’ offense ranks last in the country in total yards gained (408 yards) and points per game (8.5). They’ve had two tall tasks to open the season against Washington and Kansas State. Now with a winless FCS squad coming to town, offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s unit could really flex its muscles on Saturday.

Look for the Cougs’ front five to provide lots of time for Pinnick, who could throw open his receivers. Running backs Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi could also get going in the right direction as well.

How the Dukes win…

To hand the Cougs their first FCS loss since Cooper Kupp and Eastern Washington pulled an upset back in 2016, Duquesne could capitalize on what looks like WSU’s top weakness, its offense. If the Dukes generate the same type of quarterback pressure that the Huskies and Wildcats have produced, they could give themselves a chance.Lots more would have to go right for Duquesne, whose offense ranks nearly last in the FCS with just 6.5 points per game, but its defense figures to stand the best chance of making things interesting. Leading tacklers Luke Miller and Zach Chambers, both linebackers, would have to help pick up a turnover or two on WSU.

Key stat: 527

That’s how many yards per game the Dukes are allowing through their first two games. Duquesne has faced two challenges – longtime coach Jerry Schmitt’s group has lost to FBS Air Force and Youngstown State, the latter of which ranks No. 9 in the latest FCS Top 25 poll – but still, the results haven’t been pretty for the Dukes.

If the Cougs can gash them a similar way, WSU could roll to an easy victory on Saturday afternoon.

Biggest question

Can the Cougs’ offense roar to life in a convincing way? To make those in the WSU orbit feel better about the way this season has opened, the Cougars need to win this game by a lot, which starts with their offense. Pinnick will need lots of time in the pocket, and if he gets it, he could get more receivers – and even tight end Jack Pedersen, who has just three catches for four yards this season – involved .

“A lot of it’s just communication-wise,” Pinnick said of his conversations with Moore. “Whether he can help me, with play clock or situations, and just honing me into what’s going on on the sideline after drives. A lot of it, too, is whether we have to simplify plays or concepts, and that’s what we gotta do. But at the end of the day, our conversation has always been, ‘what can help this offense grow’ and obviously, what can he do? Like, what are we hearing that he’s not? I think this is a good relationship that me and him have that we’re able to talk with each other and establish some things that we need to work on.”

Washington State.title: What's behind WSU's offensive struggles this season? Let's check out some film
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – To ascend into Washington State’s starting lineup and become the Cougars’ starting center, the brains behind their front five, Noah Dunham had to learn to be a little more vocal around his teammates.

On his journey, a three-year path filled with ups and downs and starts and stops, Dunham found his voice earlier this year. That helped him grow closer to his teammates, many of whom have waited their turn like Dunham, and now they’re playing alongside each other.

It’s also helped Dunham address some of the problems his team is facing. Headed into a Saturday home opener against winless FCS squad Duquesne, WSU is 0-2 for the first time since 2016. The Cougars’ offense ranks last nationally in both total offense (408 yards) and points per game, 8.5, which is skewed by safety Jaylen Thomas’ pick-six last weekend against Kansas State.

In reality, the Cougars have totaled just one offensive touchdown, which is also the fewest nationwide. At WSU, that has brought one group under the microscope most: its offensive line.

“I think it’s always personal just because we’re offensive linemen,” Dunham said. “We take pride in that, and I think that’s what it comes down to. Third-and-short, whatever it is, we gotta move them past the sticks, and that’s just how it is. We play O-line, and we’re always gonna take that. It doesn’t matter the play call, who’s in the backfield – that doesn’t matter. You just gotta move the sticks.”

The problem for the Cougs is that more often than not, they have not done so. Through two weeks, their offense has converted just 2 of 21 chances on third down, one spot up from last in the country. WSU and quarterback Caden Pinnick went 0-for-9 in a season-opening Apple Cup loss, then followed up with a 2-for-12 effort last weekend in a blowout loss to Kansas State.

Pinnick and Cougar coach Kirby Moore have indicated that as much as they’re struggling on third down, many of the reasons behind that trend have more to do with first and second down. Against K-State, WSU’s average yards to go on third down was 9, an untenable number, no matter the opponent. The Cougs faced three third downs of 9-plus yards, missing on all four of those chances.

To nail down some of the patterns behind that, we’re going to examine some playson video. First, though, let’s explore this: In Pro Football Focus’ updated pass-blocking grades from Saturday’s game, four WSU offensive linemen now have grades of 0.0, the lowest possible figure: left tackle Ashton Tripp (one sack given up, five pressures), right tackle/left guard Jonny Lester (one sack given up, five pressures), left guard Kyle Martin (two pressures) and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell (two pressures).

In that game, Kansas State piled up 28 quarterback pressures, second-most nationally in Week 2 of college football, a remarkable number. Washington State now ranks last in PFF’s team pass-blocking grades, earning a figure of 17.3, which is almost 10 full points below the penultimate team.

“I thought that was a positive, seeing Jaylin out there,” Moore said, referring to Caldwell subbing in to open the second half. “He did a nice job with the reps that he had. Believe it was Nick (Bakken) got nicked up there a little bit. Kyle was a little bit nicked up going into the game. So I think all those guys need to be able to rotate, and we’re gonna need all of them up front.”

Bakken did go down in Saturday’s game, but he made a quick return, submitting the best game of any of WSU’s offensive linemen this season: 85.5 pass-blocking grade and 85.4 run-blocking grade, good for an overall offensive grade of 71.5 through two games. That ranks second among qualified Cougars, behind only Pinnick, who has logged a grade of 78.2.

Before we dive into videoclips, let’s keep this context in mind: WSU was expected to lose these first two games. The Cougars were 24.5-point underdogs against the Huskies and 18.5-point underdogs against the Wildcats. Against K-State, WSU’s offensive line faced tall tasks against pass rushers Wendell Gregory, Darien Whitaker, Travis Bates and Jordan Allen. When Pac-12 play arrives, the Cougs won’t face the same caliber of defensive linemen.

It’s also worth keeping in mind that WSU is operating without star receiver Tony Freeman, who will miss the rest of the season with a torn ACL. That removes a key piece of the Cougars’ ability to stretch the field.

To examine some of WSU’s problems on third down, let’s start with the Cougars’ first attempt, a third-and-1 run for running back Kirby Vorhees. He’s driven back for no gain, in large part because the Cougars couldn’t block Wildcat safety Koy Beasley, the first to meet him.

On the next play, the Cougars decide to go for it, which is a fine idea on fourth-and-1 on the plus side of the field. But they go with a QB keeper for Pinnick, K-State’s defense doesn’t pay any mind to running back Maxwell Woods going in motion and the Cougars can’t get it blocked for Pinnick, who is turned away at the line of scrimmage. Turnover on downs.

Late in the second quarter, the Cougs are facing third-and-6, which is a pretty obvious passing situation. Let’s set the scene: WSU’s right tackle is Lester, who spent the first four seasons of his career at the left guard spot, kicking out to tackle occasionally when injuries forced it. But this season, coaches have made him a tackle by design.

It’s interesting to take a look at how Lester has fared at the guard spots versus at the tackle spot. Last season, his first year in a starting role, many of his best-graded games in the pass-blocking department came when he played guard: 83.8 against Utah State, 77.1 against Louisiana Tech, 76.1 against North Texas, 73.8 against Idaho.

In fact, three of Lester’s four worst-graded games came when he played tackle: 54.1 against Toledo, 44.0 against Virginia, 0.0 against Oregon State.

On Saturday, playing tackle meant he had to face star edge rusher Gregory, who easily bends and beats Lester, getting home for a sack on this play in the second quarter.

Late in the second quarter, WSU has a third-and-1 in K-State territory, needing only 1 yard to keep the drive alive. But coaches dial up a deep shot for receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who was never really open, resulting in an incompletion. In what registered as a strange decision, the Cougs then punt it away on fourth-and-1.

But like Moore has mentioned after each of his WSU team’s first two losses this season, many of the Cougars’ problems on third down stem from their inability to set themselves up with a manageable distance. Early in the second quarter, looking at second-and-9, Pinnick drops back and looks deep for Woods, who also was not quite open, even out-of-bounds on his route.

One play later, WSU decides to roll out the pocket for Pinnick, buying him some time. But on this play, another problem that has surfaced before bites the Cougs: Their receivers can’t create separation. Darrius Clemons can’t do that here, and WSU goes three-and-out on its first series of the second half.

Let’s rewind a bit, going back to the first quarter, when that theme came up again. On second-and-11, Pinnick drops back to pass, but he faces almost immediate pressure because Martin is beaten by K-State defensive tackle Bates. That forces Pinnick to scramble and throw an incompletion. Two plays later, WSU kicker Jack Stevens kicks his field goal attempt too low, resulting in a block, making him 1-for-4 on field goals to open the season.

One note on Martin, who is starting for the first time in his college career: On the season, he has allowed one sack on six pressures, giving him an overall PFF pass-blocking grade of 0.0, the lowest-graded pass-blocker in the country. Caldwell has only played 32 snaps, all coming in the second half of Saturday’s game, but he has also picked up a pass-blocking grade of 0.0 on the year.

To revisit the pattern of short second-down plays, WSU suffered another early in the third quarter. The Cougars call a second-and-10 inside run for Vorhees, who gains just 2 yards, setting up his team’s offense for a third-and-8.

“It’s just tough now,” TNT color commentator Mike Golic Jr. said on the broadcast. “It feels like every drive has been play action on first down, a run on second down and then you put your offense in this third-and-long situation by having that rhythm that the defense has clearly picked up on.”

For just about every team nationwide, third-and-8 is a fairly obvious passing down, which means another chance for Gregory to gear up and go. On this play, he’s matched up with Tripp, who can’t hold him off, resulting in Pinnick taking another sack.

Tripp turned in a solid Apple Cup, finishing with a PFF pass-blocking grade of 72.9, allowing zero pressures. But thanks to a sluggish matchup with K-State, he is now at 31.5.

Can the Cougars bounce back? Without a doubt. With a convincing win over FCS Duquesne this weekend, Moore’s team could launch itself into a home matchup with Arizona the following week with a healthy dose of momentum. It’s still early for a new group still gelling and learning each other’s strengths and weaknesses.

Even so, WSU has plenty of work to do on offense. For the Cougars to get back on track, they’ll have to shore up a lot, particularly up front.

Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s home opener against Duquesne on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

In new head coach Kirby Moore’s home debut, WSU is set to host FCS Duquesne, which is coming off two straight losses to open the season. The Cougars are doing the same, so with an opportunity to kick-start an offense that ranks last nationally in total offense, this game might have a little extra meaning for the hosts.

Outside of WSU’s long-running series with nearby Idaho, it’s the Cougars’ first time hosting an FCS opponent since earning a 70-30 win over Portland State in 2024.

Where is it?

Gesa Field at Martin Stadium in Pullman.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 12:30 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

USA Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

As of Monday afternoon, WSU was around a 35.5-point favorite in most sportsbooks.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 34-7 loss to Kansas State, dropping WSU to 0-2 for the first time since 2016, the Cougars’ offense fell flat. That group did not score, the first time the program has gone scoreless on offense since 2010, and quarterback Caden Pinnick completed just 9 of 20 passes for 65 yards, becoming the first WSU QB to pass for fewer than 100 yards since Jeff Tuel did it in the same season, back when Paul Wulff was head coach.

WSU scored once, a pick-six going into halftime from safety Jaylen Thomas, who picked off two passes total in the game. But the Cougars didn’t score otherwise, totaling just 166 yards of offense, giving them 408 yards of total offense and 204 per game – both of which rank last in the country. Running backs Kirby Vorhees and Maxwell Woods combined for just 74 yards, and Vorhees lost a fumble for the second straight game.

It was also another sluggish outing from WSU’s special teams department. In the first quarter, kicker Jack Stevens sent a field -goal attempt too low, allowing it to get tipped at the line of scrimmage, giving him three misses in his first four tries to open the season. And in the second quarter, the Cougs permitted a 62-yard punt return, giving the Wildcats a chance to score a touchdown two plays later to secure a 17-0 lead.

The visitors’ defense was hardly perfect – one of the biggest problems was that WSU generated just seven pressures on K-State QB Avery Johnson – but their offense was the main culprit behind this loss. The Cougars were playing without top wide receiver Tony Freeman, who is now expected to miss the rest of the season due to a torn ACL, taking away a key component of his team’s offense and kick/punt return game.

“Well, I think you go back. Have had a lot of meetings, really getting off the flight, and then yesterday in the morning,” Moore said. “Starts back with our process of game planning, the number of reps we get in practice, how many looks we get of those during the week. Obviously, that’s gonna build confidence for the players and what could come on Saturday. Everyone being on the same page – that’s the one thing about offensive football. Gotta have all 11 working together. At the end of the day, we gotta score more points to be successful here.”

WSU also didn’t have either of its starting cornerbacks, Jalil Tucker (out with injury) and Khamari Terrell (out for undisclosed reasons). Each are expected to be available in Saturday’s game against Duquesne, Moore said.

Scouting Duquesne …

The Dukes are coming off two straight road FBS losses to open the season, a 34-0 defeat to Air Force and a 70-13 setback at the hands of Youngstown State. They rank last in the FCS in total offense, posting just 351 total yards, and they’ve also lost a pair of turnovers .

Duquesne is led by head coach Jerry Schmitt, who is in his 22nd season at the helm of the program. He’s taken the Dukes to the FCS playoffs three times in his tenure, most recently in 2023.

This year, the team’s quarterback is sixth-year journeyman Carson Camp, who started his career with three seasons at South Dakota before spending the 2023 and 2024 seasons at Sacramento State. He transferred to Southeastern Louisiana, where he threw for nearly 1,800 yards before moving over to Duquesne . In two games this fall, he has completed just 12 of 37 passes (32%) for 105 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions.

The Dukes also rank seven spots up from last in the FCS ranks in total defense, allowing an average of 526.5 yards per game.

“Offensively, they do a good job with RPOs and got an experienced quarterback. He’s entering his seventh year in college football,” Moore said. “Very solid running backs. No. 32 (Ness Davis) was an all-conference player last year, and defensively they have seven new starters, so a little bit of a new group there.”

What happened last time?

This will be the teams’ first-ever meeting.

Washington State.title: WSU WR Tony Freeman to miss rest of season with torn ACL, plus other injury updates
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State wide receiver Tony Freeman has played his final snap of the season.

Freeman is expected to miss the rest of the season with a torn ACL, coach Kirby Moore said Monday, dealing a costly blow to the Cougars’ receiving and kick return departments. A senior and a team captain, the speedy Freeman was expected to be his team’s top option on both fronts.

Freeman’s injury happened during WSU’s season-opening loss to rival Washington on Sept. 6. Freeman played just 10 snaps before going down with his injury, going to the locker room and returning in street clothes.

WSU’s medical staff is still determining Freeman’s surgery date, Moore said, adding that it’s possible Freeman returns for an extra season next fall. But that much is unclear at this point.

A year ago, Freeman started seven of 13 games, reeling in 54 passes for 590 yards and three touchdowns. In the punt return department, he also recorded an average punt return of 17.3 yards, the sixth-best mark nationwide and a WSU single-season record. He also set a program record with 415 punt return yards on the season.

Freeman’s absence figures to be another tough development for WSU’s offense, which ranks last nationally in total offense (408 yards) and points per game (8.5). In the Cougars’ loss to Kansas State on Saturday, their offense went scoreless for the first time since a a blowout loss to Arizona State in 2010, when Paul Wulff was head coach.

That’s a key reason behind the Cougars’ 0-2 start to the season, the program’s first since 2016. On Saturday, quarterback Caden Pinnick passed for just 65 yards, becoming the first WSU signal-caller since Jeff Tuel registered fewer than 100 passing yards in 2010.

A quick slot receiver, Freeman’s absence figures to push other WSU receivers into the spotlight. In Saturday’s game, Cougar wideouts Daniel Blood and Darrius Clemons combined for just 41 yards on five catches. Transfer receiver Tank Hawkins, who started the game but played only one snap, could wind up in a bigger role as well.

WSU could also ask a bit more from veteran receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who caught one pass for 11 yards against K-State. That was the Cougs’ first third-down conversion of the season.

“Darrius made a couple plays there. BG’s stepped in,” Moore said. “We gotta find ways to get them the ball. D-Blood first game, I think, didn’t get as many there in the second game. And then Jordan Dees and Tank Hawkins gotta find roles and find opportunities as we progress here.”

Other injury updates

In other injury news, WSU starting cornerbacks Khamari Terrell and Jalil Tucker are expected to be available for Saturday’s game against FCS Duquesne, Moore said. Terrell didn’t travel to Kansas State due to a concussion he suffered during practice last week, Moore said, while Tucker traveled but watched from the sideline in street clothes.

Those two absences cost the Cougars’ defense, which surrendered 487 total yards to the Wildcats, including 192 passing from quarterback Avery Johnson and another 295 rushing. WSU’s replacements on defense were Kai Rapolla and Jamarey Smith, the latter of whom moved from nickel to cornerback. Rapolla allowed four catches on five targets, according to Pro Football Focus, while Smith permitted just one catch on five targets.

It was a bit of a slow game for Rapolla, who finished with an overall PFF defense grade of just 52.2, so Terrell and Tucker’s returns should boost WSU’s defense. Tucker got hurt in the Apple Cup, when he went airborne to break up a tipped pass and a UW defender tackled him at the knees.

• WSU defensive ends Michael Hughes and Malachi Wrice are expected to miss Saturday’s game nursing their own injuries, Moore said. Hughes, who didn’t play against K-State, is expected to miss a couple weeks with a leg injury, while Wrice is considered week-to-week.

Both Hughes and Wrice are backups, but their absences could loom large for WSU, who has two stars at that position in Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk. But now the Cougars’ depth will be tested. It’s possible the Cougs ask more from defensive ends like Ben Beatty and Fernanco Lecuona (20 snaps apiece against K-State), plus Arizona transfer Eduwa Okundaye, who played 11 snaps in Manhattan.

“All those guys, we gotta rotate and be fresh up front,” Moore said, “and that’s gonna be important.”

Thomas named Pac-12 Defensive Player of the WeekIn Saturday’s game, Jaylen Thomas delivered two interceptions, including a 50-yard pick-six going into halftime. That helped him earn Pac-12 Defensive Player of the Week honors, according to a Monday release.

He’s the first WSU player with multiple interceptions in a game since Sam Lockett III had two against Arizona in November 2022. He’s also the first Cougar defender to record multiple interceptions with at least one returned for touchdown since Armani Marsh in the 2021 Apple Cup.

Thomas also became the first WSU player to post a pick-six since former linebacker Taariq Al-Uqdah did so in 2024 against Oregon State.

“I love Jaylen Thomas, just working with him on a daily basis,” Moore said. Obviously, coach (Greg) Burns had experience with him in the past (at San Jose State). He’s a student of the game. He works his tail off. He’s up on the fifth floor multiple hours outside of the players’ hours, meeting with coach Burns, talking with coach (Trent) Bray, and I think that’s shown up on the field.”
